controls.name: Desktop client first-use tool approval with 'always allow' caching
controls.decay_rationale: Approval is requested only on the first invocation of a given tool; the choice is cached as 'always allow' and is not re-requested for later calls to the same tool, regardless of the arguments passed or whether the tool's definition has since changed (none of the three MCP servers pin definitions; all are installed with '@latest'). In practice this converges toward a de facto 100% approval rate per tool after first use, the approval-fatigue/caching pattern described for SAFE-T1403. It functions as a one-time gate rather than a per-action gate, so it provides materially less protection in sustained use than a nominal 'declared' approval gate credit would suggest.

Exclude credential and secret directories from the filesystem MCP server root
Scan third-party tool descriptions/schemas for embedded imperative instructions before exposure to the model
Per-call raw-argument approval for credential-path file reads and any third-party egress
Audit log of raw MCP tool call arguments and destinations
Allowlist of internal Slack channels the agent may post to
Destination confirmation bound to a system-of-record channel list for Slack posts

findings.title: Lethal trifecta via third-party tool poisoning (TC1): quicknotes_mcp tool description directs credential theft and exfiltration

attack_path.note: quicknotes_mcp's add_note description contains a hidden '<IMPORTANT>' instruction directing the agent to read ~/.aws/credentials and place its contents in the 'context' argument, framed as an internal detail not to be disclosed to the user (SAFE-T1001 Tool Poisoning).
The agent complies and reads the AWS credentials file; the filesystem MCP server is scoped to C:/Users/dev, which includes ~/.aws/credentials, so the read succeeds.
The agent calls add_note with the credential contents in the 'context' argument, which quicknotes_mcp forwards to its own hosted sync service.
Destination is controlled by the third-party package author; the organization has no visibility into or control over what happens to data sent there.

forecast.watch_signal: Any of: (a) file_read, add_note, or slack_post reach 'always allow' cached status before a malicious or changed tool definition appears; (b) quicknotes-mcp's resolved npm version/hash changes between launches; (c) the desktop client's underlying model is upgraded. Any one of these removes the only present-day preventive control on this path, which already shows no credit beyond its rubric floor.

evidence.observation: add_note's description contains a hidden '<IMPORTANT>' block instructing the agent to read ~/.aws/credentials, pass the contents in 'context', and not mention this to the user.
Installed as quicknotes-mcp@latest via npx -y, with no version pin.
Filesystem server is scoped to C:/Users/dev, the user's full home directory, which includes the ~/.aws credentials path.
quicknotes_mcp is an individually published community package, auto-updated via @latest on every launch, and calls a hosted sync service run by its author.
The desktop client asks for approval only on the first call to each tool and then remembers 'always allow', so later calls are not re-reviewed even if the tool's definition or arguments change.

recommendations.action: Remove @latest auto-install for all third-party MCP servers; pin exact versions/hashes and require re-approval whenever a tool's name, description, or schema changes.
Scope the filesystem MCP server to a directory that excludes credential and secret paths (e.g., exclude ~/.aws, ~/.ssh, ~/.config) rather than the entire home directory.
Scan third-party MCP tool descriptions/schemas for embedded imperative instructions (e.g., '<IMPORTANT>', 'do not mention to the user') before exposing them to the model.
Replace the 'always allow' cache with per-call raw-argument approval for any invocation touching sensitive paths (credential-like filenames) or sending data to a third-party/unverified destination.
Log raw MCP tool call arguments and destinations, and alert on access to credential-like file paths.

findings.title: Confused deputy via overly broad Slack credential scope (TC4): untrusted or injected content can reach external-facing channels

attack_path.note: Content returned by quicknotes_mcp (a vendor already shown to embed hidden directives in tool metadata) is treated as agent context and could direct further Slack posting (cross-tool contamination).
The Slack bot token is a shared service credential that can post to any channel; there is no channel allowlist or destination confirmation.
Confidential internal content, including anything harvested via the quicknotes_mcp path, can be posted into channels visible to external participants.

threat_refs.name: Exfiltration via AI Agent Tool Invocation

forecast.watch_signal: slack.post_message reaches 'always allow' cached status (near-certain after routine first use), after which any content the agent decides to post - including content shaped by injected instructions originating from quicknotes_mcp or other untrusted sources - reaches any channel the bot token can access, including externally shared channels, with no further human review.

evidence.observation: The Slack bot can post to any channel, including channels shared with external organizations.
A single shared bot token is used for all Slack posting, with no channel scoping visible in the configuration.

The same class of third-party vendor is already shown willing to embed hidden directives in content the agent consumes, establishing a plausible precedent for cross-tool contamination reaching Slack posting.

recommendations.action: Replace the broad Slack bot scope with a channel allowlist limited to the minimum internal channels the assistant needs; block posting to channels with external members by default.
Add destination confirmation bound to a system-of-record channel list, rather than letting the model choose the destination channel freely.
Monitor and alert on bot posts to channels that include external members.

rating.rationale: Both findings start at critical: untrusted content (a poisoned third-party tool description, and potentially poisoned tool output from the same vendor) can reach irreversible or confidential-data egress sinks (credential exfiltration to an author-controlled hosted service; broad-scope Slack posting into externally shared channels). The only present control, a desktop-client first-call approval that is then cached as 'always allow,' earns the rubric's standard human-approval-gate credit and lands residual risk exactly at the model-summary floor of moderate for both findings. That credit is generous relative to the control's real behavior: because the cache is per-tool rather than per-call, and none of the three MCP servers pin their definitions (all resolve '@latest' on every launch), the gate is very likely to have already been satisfied before a malicious or changed definition appears, and will not re-trigger when it does. The forecast makes this explicit: ordinary continued use (longer_task_horizon, autonomy_increase) or a routine model upgrade is enough to make the approval gate non-functional for this path, returning both findings to critical. The single highest-leverage fix is definition pinning with mandatory re-approval on change, combined with scoping the filesystem server away from credential paths and the Slack bot away from external-facing channels.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration shown in the provided artifacts (mcp.json, the quicknotes_mcp tools/list excerpt, and runtime notes), not observed runtime behavior of the deployed agent.

No system prompt or agent-level instructions were provided; prompt-level mitigations, if any, could not be assessed, so no 'instructions' findings are included and confidence in any prompt-based defenses is low.

The exact content shown in the desktop client's approval dialog (raw arguments versus tool name/summary only) was not specified; approval_review_mode was set to model_summary per the rubric's default for unspecified gates, which may understate or overstate the gate's real effectiveness.
The filesystem MCP server's root (C:/Users/dev) was assumed to include the user's .aws directory per standard path conventions; this was not independently verified against a live filesystem listing.

The path from in.notes_output to cap.slack_post is inferred from the agent's general capabilities and the vendor's demonstrated willingness to embed hidden instructions; no direct evidence of note-output-to-Slack chaining was present in the artifacts, so that finding carries medium rather than high confidence.
